idiom_name: tag structs in an inheritance ladder + a detail overload set + one public forwarder
implementation_notes: The canonical realization: an empty tag type per category, related by inheritance (std::input_iterator_tag -> forward -> bidirectional -> random_access -> contiguous), obtained from a trait (std::iterator_traits<It>::iterator_category) or from std::integral_constant for boolean properties (true_type/false_type/bool_constant). Overload resolution picks the most-derived match and degrades to the nearest base tag, so the ladder doubles as a priority chain and as the fallback mechanism. Choose it when the ladder must be extended by users via ADL, when each path must be separately overloadable, or when the toolchain is older than C++17.
pitfalls: A missing level compiles as a promotion to a base tag: the algorithm silently becomes slower (or wrong) with no diagnostic, so every level must be audited.
The tag parameter must stay unnamed and unused; storing it or turning it into a runtime value re-introduces the cost the pattern removes.

Mixing the ladder with return-type SFINAE multiplies the levels: every overload must additionally be enabled or disabled by hand, and both mechanisms report failures against the ladder's own signatures instead of the caller's type.
sources: cppreference, std::input_iterator_tag ... std::contiguous_iterator_tag (the standard tag ladder), https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/iterator/iterator_tags
foonathan, Controlling overload resolution #3: Tag dispatching (integral_constant and priority chains), https://www.foonathan.net/2015/11/overload-resolution-3/
Arne Mertz, Tag Dispatch: Useful Empty Classes, https://arne-mertz.de/2016/10/tag-dispatch/

variants.name: Priority tag chain (priority_tag<N> with an unconstrained fallback)
variants.idiom_name: priority_tag<N> ladder, levels eliminated by SFINAE, fallback level unconstrained
variants.implementation_notes: When the decision is 'use the most specific implementation this type can support, otherwise the next best', the tag encodes rank rather than semantics: priority_tag<N> derives from priority_tag<N-1>, each level's overload is SFINAE-eliminated when the type cannot support it, and the last level is unconstrained so that types with no capability still compile. This replaces stacked std::enable_if negation (each level would otherwise have to restate the negation of every higher level's condition) and is the form documented with Boost-style priority_tag usage.
pitfalls: The fallback level must accept every tag: adding a requires-clause or SFINAE condition to it turns 'no capability' into a hard error.

Amplifying the chain is silent: an overload filtered out by SFINAE does not fail, it just selects the next level, so a capability that disappeared unnoticed shows up as a behaviour change rather than a compile error.
Nested priority chains on more than one parameter are compared lexicographically per parameter and can tie; use named tags for two-dimensional dispatch.
sources: Tag Dispatch idiom reference: priority chains ('prefer A over B over C without SFINAE gymnastics'; the fallback must be unconstrained; multi-axis caveat), https://bigcpp.com/reference/idioms/tag-dispatch
foonathan, Controlling overload resolution #3: Tag dispatching (tag types related by inheritance create an overload priority chain), https://www.foonathan.net/2015/11/overload-resolution-3/

variants.name: Concept subsumption (C++20 constraint ranking)
variants.idiom_name: constrained overloads ranked by concept subsumption instead of tag inheritance
variants.implementation_notes: The standard's successor to the tag ladder: constrained overloads are ranked by subsumption (std::random_access_iterator subsumes std::bidirectional_iterator subsumes std::input_iterator), so the same 'most specific match with a graceful fallback' behaviour emerges from the constraint graph rather than from struct inheritance, with descriptive diagnostics and no tag types at all. Choose it for new code when the levels can be expressed as concepts; keep tag dispatch where users must add paths by name via ADL or where the ladder is not expressible as constraints.
pitfalls: Subsumption is a property of the constraint *form* (atomic constraints from concept definitions named in the same way), not of logical strength: two constraints that are equivalent but written differently do not subsume and the call becomes ambiguous.
Overloads that are not mutually exclusive by subsumption silently become ambiguous, so the levels usually need explicit requires (!std::random_access_iterator<I>) guards.
Concepts cannot replace every tag: a choice that must be extended by user-written overloads in other namespaces (ADL) has no concept analogue.
sources: Tag Dispatch idiom reference: C++20 concepts replicate the tag-dispatch hierarchy through concept subsumption; keep tag dispatch for open-world extension, pre-C++20 targets and unclear subsumption graphs, https://bigcpp.com/reference/idioms/tag-dispatch

Wikibooks, More C++ Idioms - Tag Dispatching: 'C++20 added concepts and requires statements, which entirely eliminates the need for tag dispatching where the constraints include both A and A && B or both A and A || B', https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Tag_Dispatching
